principles: A probation opened by being shut out
Letting only the right thing trouble you

world_behind.title: The worry is named as an objection
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has Corianton calling it unjust that a sinner should be sent to misery. Alma states his son's position accurately before answering it.

world_behind.title: This is the last of three answers
world_behind.text: Alma 40 took the resurrection, Alma 41 took restoration, and Alma 42 takes justice. The charges to Corianton run four chapters, three of them replies to questions.

world_behind.title: Alma argues from Eden
world_behind.text: Verses 2 and 3 give the cherubim and the flaming sword, and verse 5 says what would have followed if Adam had reached the tree. The doctrine is built out of a narrative his son knows.

world_behind.title: The cost of no death is stated plainly
world_behind.text: Verse 5 says the word of God would have been void and the plan frustrated. Alma treats the expulsion as the thing that made repentance possible.

world_behind.title: God would cease to be God appears three times
world_behind.text: Verses 13, 22, and 25 all use it as the reductio. Alma is testing each proposal by whether it would unmake God.

world_behind.title: Mercy and justice are given claims
world_behind.text: Verse 24 has justice exercising all his demands and mercy claiming all her own. The language is legal, and neither is described as overriding the other.

world_behind.title: The charge ends without a farewell
world_behind.text: Alma 37 and Alma 38 both close with farewell; Alma 42 closes with a commission and a prayer. Alma 43 begins the war.

words.text: The guardians placed at the garden. The record uses this form three times; the King James Bible uses cherubims sixty-five times and this spelling never. Alma sets them with the flaming sword as the thing that made a probation possible.

Treated at Alma 12:24, where Alma first gave this life as a probation. Here he uses it three times in ten verses and pairs it with preparatory, which makes the interval both a test and a getting ready.
To satisfy, to pacify a claim. The record uses it once and the King James Bible once, where Jacob sends gifts ahead to appease Esau. Alma uses it of the atonement satisfying the demands of justice.
Treated at 2 Nephi 2:10, where Lehi says a punishment is affixed opposite the plan of happiness. Alma repeats the word three times and builds the argument of verses 17 through 22 on it.

A created being, as the object of a legal claim. It appears eight times in the record, and the King James Bible twenty-nine. Alma uses it twice in two verses, in the sense of the party a law has a claim upon.
Ruling influence, the power to govern. The word occurs once in scripture. Alma asks for justice, mercy, and long-suffering to rule his son's heart, which puts all three in charge at once.

phrases.term: Ye do try to suppose that it is injustice that the sinner should be consigned to a state of misery
phrases.text: Alma states the objection in his son's own terms. The verb try is pointed: Corianton is working at the supposition rather than holding it, and Alma answers it as a real argument.

phrases.term: There was a time granted unto man to repent, yea, a probationary time
phrases.text: The conclusion Alma draws from the flaming sword. Being shut out of the tree is what created an interval, and the interval is what makes repentance possible.

phrases.term: The word of God would have been void, and the great plan of salvation would have been frustrated
phrases.text: Alma names what was at stake in the expulsion. Eating from the tree would have made a promise false and a plan impossible, so the guard is described as protecting both.

phrases.term: They became subjects to follow after their own will
phrases.text: The result of being cut off temporally and spiritually. Alma gives the fall as a change in what a person is subject to, which sets up the carnal state of verse 10.

phrases.term: The work of justice could not be destroyed; if so, God would cease to be God
phrases.text: The chapter's test, used three times. Alma checks each proposal by asking whether it would unmake God, and this is the first of the three places he applies it.

phrases.term: God himself atoneth for the sins of the world, to bring about the plan of mercy
phrases.text: The center of the answer. Alma has said mercy cannot destroy justice, and here he names the way both are satisfied, with God himself as the one who does it.

phrases.term: How could a man repent except he should sin? How could he sin if there was no law?
phrases.text: Three questions running backward to a foundation. Alma reaches law, then punishment, then the possibility of fear, and builds the case forward again in verses 19 through 22.

phrases.term: Mercy claimeth the penitent, and mercy cometh because of the atonement
phrases.text: A chain of five links: mercy, atonement, resurrection, presence of God, judgment. Alma runs it in one sentence so the connection between them is visible.

phrases.term: Justice exerciseth all his demands, and also mercy claimeth all which is her own
phrases.text: Both are satisfied in full and neither is reduced. Alma's conclusion from it is narrow: none but the truly penitent are saved.

phrases.term: Do ye suppose that mercy can rob justice? I say unto you, Nay; not one whit
phrases.text: Alma answers the objection head on. The phrase not one whit refuses even a partial exchange, and the sentence ends with the same test about God ceasing to be God.

phrases.term: Let these things trouble you no more, and only let your sins trouble you
phrases.text: Alma redirects his son's distress. Four chapters of doctrine end by telling him which worry is worth keeping and what it should produce.

phrases.term: Do not endeavor to excuse yourself in the least point
phrases.text: Alma names what the objection was for. Denying the justice of God had been a way of making room, and this sentence closes it.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: The objection is quoted before it is answered
verses.text: Alma states his son's position in his son's terms: "ye do try to suppose that it is injustice that the sinner should be consigned to a state of misery." Everything that follows can be checked against that one sentence: it names the complaint, attributes it to Corianton, and concedes that he cannot understand the answer yet. Alma does not correct the wording before he argues with it.

verses.label: v. 2–6
verses.title: He answers a question about justice by going to Eden
verses.text: Tree is confined to verses 2 through 6 and drops out of the chapter for good. Before any argument about the sinner, Alma establishes a cherubim, a flaming sword, and a man kept from eating and living forever, which buys him the one thing the argument needs: "a time granted unto man to repent" (v. 4). The premise Alma builds on is a garden, not a principle.

cites.quote: a time granted unto man to repent

spans.text: a time granted unto man to repent

verses.label: v. 17–21
verses.title: The tightest argument is the one he refuses to assert
verses.text: All six of the chapter's questions fall between verses 17 and 25, and three of them are in verse 17 alone: how could a man repent, how could he sin, how could there be a law. Alma reaches the hinge of his case and stops making claims, handing the conclusions to his son to draw.

verses.label: v. 22–25
verses.title: The verb that decides it
verses.text: Claimeth is confined to verses 22 to 24: repentance mercy claimeth, otherwise justice claimeth the creature and executeth the law. Alma settles a dispute about fairness by asking which party holds a claim, a legal question rather than a moral one, and then stakes the whole answer on a single consequence he is willing to state three times: "God would cease to be God" (v. 13, again at 22 and 25).

verses.label: v. 27–28
verses.title: The one verse that is neither argument nor command
verses.text: After twenty-six verses of reasoning, "whosoever will come may come and partake of the waters of life freely; and whosoever will not is not compelled to come." The chapter's tightest logical machine issues in a verse with no if in it.

verses.label: v. 29–31
verses.title: He stops arguing and starts telling him what to do
verses.text: The register turns imperative and does not turn back: let these things trouble you no more, deny the justice of God no more, go thy way, declare the word. A chapter that opened by quoting a question closes without asking one. Its last phrase is "the great plan of mercy," a name Alma could not have reached for in verse 1, because mercy had not yet entered the argument.

chapter.title: The objection is stated fairly before it is answered
chapter.text: Verse 1 states the objection in the son's own terms, "ye do try to suppose that it is injustice that the sinner should be consigned to a state of misery," and names it as a worry rather than an error. The reply runs from verse 2 to verse 30, twenty-nine verses. The same courtesy is extended to Antionah at Alma 12:20–27 and to Corianton twice more in this chapter, at verses 16 and 25, where his supposed positions are restated before being answered.

chapter.title: The doctrine is built from a story
chapter.text: Verses 2 and 3 quote Genesis 3:22–24 closely, "cherubim, and a flaming sword which turned every way," and "lest he should put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat and live forever." Every step of the argument from verse 4 onward is tied back to that scene rather than to a general principle. Alma 12:21–26 built the identical case from the same three verses of Genesis for a different hearer, so the record uses one passage twice as the ground of one doctrine.

chapter.title: Exclusion is what made repentance possible
chapter.text: Verse 4 names the result of the exclusion as a period, "there was a time granted unto man to repent, yea, a probationary time," and verse 5 states the alternative outcome, that Adam "would have lived forever... having no space for repentance," with two further consequences, that "the word of God would have been void" and the plan "frustrated." The barrier of Genesis 3:24 is read three times over as what made repentance possible, and the reading is reached by supposing the opposite case rather than by asserting the point.

chapter.title: One test is applied three times
chapter.text: God would cease to be God. Alma uses it at verses 13, 22, and 25, each time against a different proposal, and the whole argument rests on it.

chapter.title: Justice and mercy are both given full claims
chapter.text: Neither is softened. Alma's answer is that the atonement satisfies both completely, and he refuses even a partial trade between them.

chapter.title: The chain in verse 23 is the answer in miniature
chapter.text: Mercy, atonement, resurrection, presence, judgment. Five links in a single line, which is how Alma shows they are not separate mercies.

chapter.title: The invitation is left genuinely open
chapter.text: Whoever will come may; whoever will not is not compelled. Alma places the whole doctrine of justice beside an unforced offer.

chapter.title: The charge ends with an assignment
chapter.text: No farewell, unlike the other two. Alma tells his son he is called of God, sends him to preach with truth and soberness, and the war begins in the next chapter.

applications.title: State the objection before answering it
applications.text: Alma repeated his son's position in his son's own terms and called it a worry rather than an error. Before you answer a challenge, say it back in a form the person who raised it would accept.

applications.title: Look for the mercy in the hard part
applications.text: The flaming sword is read as the thing that created a time to repent. When some restriction in your life looks purely like exclusion, ask what it is holding open.

applications.title: Argue by supposing the opposite
applications.text: Alma tests the case by running the alternative: if Adam had eaten of the tree, there would have been no space for repentance and the word would have been void. When you cannot see why a thing had to be so, work out what would follow if it were not.

applications.title: Keep both claims when you cannot reconcile them
applications.text: "Justice exerciseth all his demands, and also mercy claimeth all which is her own," and then the question, "do ye suppose that mercy can rob justice? I say unto you, Nay." Alma refuses to buy one by weakening the other. Some pairs of true things stay in tension, and the honest move is to hold both.

applications.title: Leave the door unlatched in both directions
applications.text: "Whosoever will come may come... and whosoever will not come the same is not compelled to come." The invitation and the freedom to decline are stated together, in the same breath. When you offer something, make the refusal genuinely available or the offer is not one.

applications.title: Keep the right trouble
applications.text: Alma told his son to stop worrying about one thing and start being troubled by another. Distress is not the problem; distress about the wrong subject is.

applications.title: Stop using a belief as an excuse
applications.text: Denying God's justice had a function for Corianton. When a doctrinal difficulty of yours has a convenient consequence, deal with the consequence first.

applications.title: End by giving the person a job
applications.text: After thirty verses of doctrine the instruction is one sentence: "go thy way, declare the word with truth and soberness." A correction that stops at being right leaves the person nowhere to put it.

questions.text: What do I try to suppose because the alternative would cost me something?
What time have I been granted that I have been treating as ordinary?
What would I have to believe about God for my current excuse to work?
Do I want mercy for myself and justice for other people?
What is keeping me from partaking freely?
Which of my troubles is worth keeping?
Where am I excusing myself in the least point?
